title: The Battle of Kadesh
objective: After this level you can explain the battle and the peace treaty that followed.
summary: At Kadesh, around 1274 BCE, Ramesses II fought the Hittites to a draw and advertised it as a victory. Years later the two powers signed the oldest peace treaty whose text survives.

cards.headline: Ramesses carved his great victory at Kadesh into temple walls. It wasn’t one.
cards.body: His reliefs show him single-handedly defeating the enemy. The battle was real, and so was the danger. It’s the ending that got edited.

cards.headline: Walking into a trap
cards.body: Around 1274 BCE, Ramesses marched into Syria to fight the Hittites, Egypt’s great rival, under their king Muwatallis, near the city of Kadesh on the Orontes River. Men posing as Hittite deserters fed him false information; they were enemy agents. A surprise Hittite attack scattered his army, in one of the largest chariot battles ever fought.

cards.headline: A draw, with good publicity
cards.body: Ramesses regrouped and counterattacked, and the day ended in what historians call an honorable draw. Neither side won outright, and Ramesses did not take Kadesh. Back home, though, he claimed a great victory, and his temple reliefs show him beating the enemy single-handed. Ancient spin, carved in stone.
cards.callout: What happened: a draw. What he carved: a victory.

cards.headline: Peace, in writing
cards.body: Years later, Ramesses and a new Hittite king, Hattusili III, made peace. Theirs is the oldest known peace treaty whose text survives, made as between equal great powers, with the same promises on both sides: lasting peace, nonaggression, extradition and mutual help. Both versions survive: the Egyptian one on temple walls at Karnak, the Hittite one on a clay tablet from Hattusa. A replica hangs at the United Nations, near the Security Council.

mascot.line: Two old enemies, one treaty, and a copy right outside the room where nations still argue.

cards.headline: Kadesh: fought and settled
learned: Around 1274 BCE, Ramesses fought the Hittites at Kadesh
He was ambushed, and the battle ended in a draw
His temple reliefs show a great victory anyway
The later peace treaty is the oldest whose text survives

questions.prompt: Which empire did Ramesses II fight at the Battle of Kadesh?

options.label: The Romans
options.rationale: Rome came more than a thousand years later.

options.label: The Persians
options.rationale: His enemy at Kadesh was the Hittite king Muwatallis.

options.label: The Greeks
options.rationale: The battle was against the Hittites.

questions.explanation: Ramesses fought the Hittites under King Muwatallis near Kadesh, on the Orontes River in Syria.

questions.prompt: Ramesses’ reliefs show him winning Kadesh single-handed. What do historians conclude?

options.label: He won an easy and total victory over them
options.rationale: He was ambushed, and nobody won outright.

options.label: The battle never took place
options.rationale: It was real, and both sides recorded it.

options.label: It was a draw; neither side won outright

questions.explanation: Kadesh ended in an honorable draw: Ramesses survived the ambush but did not take the city, then advertised it as a victory.

questions.prompt: Kadesh ended in a draw. How did the Egyptian-Hittite treaty that followed treat the two sides?

options.label: As winner and loser, with Egypt collecting tribute
options.rationale: Its promises were the same on both sides.

options.label: As equal great powers, with the same promises on both sides
As a Hittite takeover of Egypt
As a truce that lasted only a year

questions.explanation: After a battle neither could win, Ramesses and Hattusili III made peace as equals, with reciprocal promises.
